text_en: Kera opens a casebook on a clear table. Three diagrams show roads already known, and threats already met.
Three cases. No new alarm. No patients needed for demonstration.
An excellent beginning for a training plan.
Are we reading or trying another way through?
Both. A diagram is less convincing when nobody can use it.
Then we keep the case separate from the people who lived it.
The book stays in the archive. The exercise opens as a reconstruction, not as another journey in their day.
A reaching threat asks you to look past the first body.
A heavy front asks you not to forget the body nearest you.
Choose one emphasis. You will still see the other.
Keep enough room to recover. There is no virtue in panicking early.
Steady front. Recorded. It is a choice, not a score.
Check who can reach past the line before choosing the nearest target.
Reaching threat. Recorded. The diagram will not hide it.
A supporting enemy can be stopped early. Or its pressure can be outlasted while we keep the party ready.
The case must be readable either way. Nobody needs an answer we hid in the notes.
That includes the author of the notes.
Then I will watch where the support can be reached.
And keep the front ready while you choose it.
Then read the incoming action before spending your recovery.
An economical answer. I approve when it does not get anyone killed.
First case. Look at the whole line before picking the first target.
The nearest threat is visible. So is the one behind it.
Winning slowly is permitted. Failing to notice pressure is what we are practicing against.
The first case opens on its own. No wound from another exercise follows into it.
The case is complete. You can try another line without rewriting this one.
Keep the chosen emphasis beside the result. Victory alone does not tell us what we intended.
The book would become shorter if it did.
It would become less useful.
The next diagram is its own exercise, with the party ready to begin again.
Second case. The pressure has a source. Read its intent before choosing your response.
You may remove it early or stay ready while it acts. The exercise must allow both.
Do not confuse a slower victory with a failed one.
And do not confuse the nearest enemy with the source.
The second diagram opens without carrying wounds from the first.
Enough pressure to read. Enough room to answer.
The same pressure should leave room for more than one answer.
The people in the original case could not try another answer. Our notes must remember that.
The notes keep the exercise separate from its source.
Last case. The front question and the support question arrive together.
Look beyond the first threat without abandoning the people in front.
Keep the party ready without letting the pressure become invisible.
The notes are not asking you to be fast. They are asking you to keep both questions in sight.
The final reconstruction opens on its own, with the chosen threats in sight.
The casebook shows the chosen emphasis beside three completed exercises.
Holding the front is useful when it leaves room for someone else to answer the support.
A front that lasts long enough for the next decision. That is the intended lesson.
The farther threat needs attention before distance makes it look harmless.
And the people in front still need room to stay ready while you choose it.
You can close the book. Another profile will still be here.
And the clinic will still need its table.
Try another case when you want another answer. Not because a bell tells you to hurry back.
A useful exercise. No one had to make the road dangerous again.
Kera closes the diagrams. Outside the exercise, the archive remains an archive.
